questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A medication slows the transporter that clears serotonin from the synaptic cleft. What happens to signaling at that synapse?

options.text: Serotonin keeps binding receptors longer
Serotonin is released in smaller amounts
options.misconception: assumes a clearance block also reduces transmitter release

options.text: The receptors close permanently
options.misconception: believes receptor openness is permanently altered by the drug

options.text: The postsynaptic cell cannot fire at all
options.misconception: concludes silence when the effect is prolonged activation

questions.explanation: Blocking reuptake leaves transmitter in the cleft, so receptor activation is prolonged and strengthened. Vesicle release continues normally, receptors still close when they close, and the postsynaptic cell becomes more rather than less likely to fire.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if the cleanup crew stops working.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A stroke at the lowest part of the brainstem, just above the spinal cord, stops breathing and heartbeat. Which structure was damaged?

options.text: The medulla oblongata
The temporal lobe cortex
options.misconception: attributes vital control to a hearing and language region

options.text: The thalamic relay nuclei
options.misconception: credits a sensory relay station with running the heartbeat

options.text: The cerebellum at the back
options.misconception: assigns breathing and cardiac control to a coordination structure

questions.explanation: The medulla at the base of the brainstem carries the reflex centers for breathing, heartbeat, and blood pressure, so damage there is life-threatening. The thalamus relays sensation, the cerebellum coordinates movement, and the temporal cortex handles hearing and language.
questions.hint: Which structure sits at the very base of the brainstem?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A diagram of a hand touching a hot surface numbers four events: 1 sensory receptor fires, 2 spinal interneurons fire, 3 motor neurons fire, 4 the arm withdraws. Which statement about that sequence is accurate?

options.text: Withdrawal can begin before the brain registers pain
The brain must issue the command for withdrawal
options.misconception: places the motor command at the cortex rather than the spinal cord

options.text: The motor neurons fire before the interneurons
options.misconception: reverses the order of the interneuron and motor steps

options.text: The sensory receptor is activated after withdrawal
options.misconception: moves detection to the end of the sequence shown

questions.explanation: A spinal reflex arc runs from receptor to interneurons to motor neurons entirely inside the cord, so the movement starts while the signal is still traveling up to the brain. That is why a person feels the pain only after the hand has already pulled away.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A region of cortex that is neither primary sensory nor primary motor integrates memory, attention, and reasoning across several inputs. What is that region called?

options.text: Association cortex
The primary visual strip
options.misconception: confuses a first-stage sensory station with an integrative region

options.text: The somatosensory strip
options.misconception: mistakes a touch map for a region that combines many inputs

options.text: The motor homunculus
options.misconception: assigns higher-order integration to a movement map

questions.explanation: Association cortex links outputs of several primary areas, which is what supports memory, attention, and reasoning. The visual strip, the touch strip, and the motor homunculus are primary stations that each handle one kind of input or output rather than integrating across them.
questions.hint: The name says what it does with information.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a compound that blocks adenosine receptors raises alertness instead of causing drowsiness.

answer.exemplar: Adenosine builds up across the waking day and acts on receptors that suppress neuronal firing, which produces the feeling of sleepiness. A compound that occupies those receptors without activating them prevents adenosine from delivering that message, so the suppression never arrives. The cell keeps firing at its usual rate and the person stays awake. The effect is a blockade of a drowsiness signal, not a direct injection of energy or a change in the neuron's resting potential.

questions.explanation: The compound does not excite neurons directly; it removes the brake that adenosine applies. Blocking an inhibitory signal therefore raises arousal, which is why this class of substances keeps people awake.
questions.hint: Ask what signal is being prevented from arriving.

questions.stem: Which transmitter, arising from neurons clustered in a narrow band along the brainstem's midline, is most closely tied to mood, sleep, and appetite?

options.text: Serotonin from the raphe nuclei
Acetylcholine from the basal forebrain
options.misconception: credits a learning and arousal transmitter with mood and appetite

options.text: Norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus
options.misconception: attributes mood and appetite to an alertness-generating system

options.text: Glycine from spinal interneurons
options.misconception: names a spinal inhibitory transmitter with no mood role

questions.explanation: Serotonin neurons of the raphe nuclei project widely and modulate mood, sleep, and appetite. The basal forebrain cholinergic system supports learning and arousal, the locus coeruleus norepinephrine system supports alertness, and glycine inhibits movement circuits in the spinal cord.
questions.hint: The source neurons sit along the seam of the brainstem.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A table lists three patients: one with cerebellar damage is unsteady while walking but feels normal, one with parietal damage cannot locate touch on one arm, and one with temporal damage cannot understand speech. What conclusion follows from the pattern?

options.text: Different structures carry different functions
Any cortical damage gives the same loss

options.text: All three deficits come from one lesion site
options.misconception: collapses three separate locations into a single site

options.text: Damage always impairs sensation only
options.misconception: ignores the unsteady movement produced by cerebellar damage

questions.explanation: Each patient loses a different ability, so structure and function map onto each other rather than being interchangeable. The deficits are not identical, the lesions are in different places, and one row shows a motor coordination problem rather than a sensory one.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: After weeks of taking a drug that blocks a receptor, a patient stops abruptly and the opposite symptoms appear strongly. What best explains those withdrawal symptoms?

options.text: The system adapted to the long blockade
The drug permanently destroyed the receptors
options.misconception: claims irreversible damage where adaptation and recovery occur

options.text: The receptors multiplied during the treatment
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the receptor adaptation

options.text: The transmitter was replaced by a different one
options.misconception: invents a chemical substitution that does not occur

questions.explanation: Chronic blockade leads the synapse to change receptor numbers or sensitivity so signaling is restored, and when the drug is removed those changes unbalance the system in the opposite direction. Receptors are not destroyed, their numbers do not simply multiply, and the transmitter is not replaced by another one.
questions.hint: Ask how a system compensates for a signal that has been muted.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A motor cortex diagram shows the toes drawn at the top of a strip, the hand in the middle, and the face at the bottom. What does the ordering show?

options.text: Body parts are arranged in an orderly map
Each body part has its own separate lobe
options.misconception: invents one lobe per body part rather than a shared strip

options.text: The map is identical on both hemispheres
options.misconception: ignores that each hemisphere mostly maps the opposite side

options.text: Body parts are scattered in random order
options.misconception: denies the orderly arrangement the drawing shows

questions.explanation: Neighboring body regions are represented by neighboring cortical sites, which is why the strip runs from toes to face in sequence. Body parts do not each get their own lobe, each hemisphere maps mostly the opposite side of the body, and the arrangement is orderly rather than random.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how the body mobilizes energy during a sudden threat, naming the branch involved and one organ effect it produces.

answer.exemplar: A threat activates the sympathetic branch, which sends signals through the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline into the blood. Heart rate and blood pressure rise so blood reaches the muscles faster, the airways widen to take in more oxygen, and stored glucose is released from the liver so muscle has fuel. Digestion and other non-urgent processes slow down because blood is redirected toward the muscles. Together these changes prepare the body to act, and the parasympathetic branch reverses them once the threat passes.

questions.explanation: The sympathetic branch and adrenaline act together to redirect resources toward action. Naming the branch plus one effect, such as a faster heartbeat, shows how the nervous and endocrine systems cooperate in one response.
questions.hint: Name the branch, then describe one thing it does to the heart or the airways.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A study compares three agonists that activate the same receptor: drug 1 produces half the maximal response at 2 milligrams, drug 2 at 20 milligrams, and drug 3 at 200 milligrams. Which inference is best?

options.text: Drug 1 is the most potent of the three
Drug 3 is the most potent of the three
options.misconception: reads a larger required dose as greater potency, a direct reversal

options.text: All three have identical efficacy at the receptor
options.misconception: confuses potency, a dose needed, with ceiling efficacy of response

options.text: Drug 2 cannot produce any response at all
options.misconception: denies the effect recorded for the middle dose curve

questions.explanation: Potency is how little drug is needed to reach a given effect, so the compound reaching half the maximal response at the lowest dose is the most potent. Efficacy, the ceiling of the response, is a separate question these data do not answer, and none of the curves is flat.
questions.hint: Ask how much of each drug it takes to reach the same level.

questions.stem: A person falls into a deep sleep when a small stem region that filters incoming messages is damaged. Which structure's job is that filtering and arousal?

The motor association cortex

options.misconception: names a fiber bridge between hemispheres as the arousal source

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A patient has low dopamine affecting movement, and separately low norepinephrine causing drowsiness. Which pairing of transmitter and function is correct?

options.text: Dopamine for movement, norepinephrine for arousal
Dopamine for arousal, norepinephrine for movement
options.misconception: swaps the two roles so each does the other's job

options.text: Dopamine for sleep onset, norepinephrine for balance
options.misconception: gives both transmitters jobs that belong to other systems

options.text: Both transmitters carry sensory touch signals
options.misconception: assigns a somatosensory role to two modulatory messengers

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: At the same synapse, compound A mimics the transmitter and compound B blocks its receptor. Which pair of effects is expected?

options.text: A amplifies signaling and B silences it
A silences signaling and B amplifies it
options.misconception: swaps the agonist and antagonist roles so each does the opposite

options.text: Both compounds amplify signaling
options.misconception: treats a receptor blocker as if it activated the receptor

options.text: Both compounds silence signaling
options.misconception: treats a mimicking compound as if it blocked the receptor

questions.explanation: An agonist produces the transmitter's own effect, so signaling rises; an antagonist occupies the receptor without activating it, so signaling falls. Swapping the two mislabels well-established drug categories, and neither compound is simply interchangeable with the other.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a touch map on cortex before and after a finger is lost; the neighboring digits take over the vacated area. What does the shift demonstrate?

options.text: Cortical maps can reorganize with use
Cortical maps are fixed from birth
options.misconception: denies reorganization that the before and after panels show

options.text: The lost finger's area was destroyed permanently
options.misconception: claims permanent loss where the map shifted to new input

options.text: The shift shows the map spreading randomly
options.misconception: misreads an orderly neighbor takeover as random spread

questions.explanation: The panels show neighboring digits expanding into territory the lost digit no longer occupies, which is cortical reorganization driven by the remaining input. The map is not fixed, the area is not permanently destroyed, and the takeover is by adjacent representations rather than random.
questions.hint: Compare the two panels and ask what changed.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Design an experiment that determines whether a new compound works by blocking a receptor or by slowing transmitter reuptake.

answer.exemplar: Apply measured pulses of transmitter at a fixed synapse and record the postsynaptic response. Then add the compound and repeat the same pulses. If it blocks the receptor, the same transmitter produces a smaller response at every dose, and adding more transmitter can overcome the block proportionally. If it slows reuptake, the transmitter that was already added persists longer, so the response rises in duration and reaches higher values, and the cleft concentration measured by a sensor stays elevated afterward. Using a second group where reuptake transporters are removed strengthens the conclusion, because the compound loses its effect there.

questions.explanation: The two mechanisms differ in profile: blockade reduces the response to a fixed transmitter amount, while reuptake inhibition prolongs and enlarges the response. Comparing response size, duration, and sensitivity to added transmitter separates the two.
questions.hint: Ask what each mechanism predicts about response size and duration.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A classmate claims that smell reaches the cortex without passing through the thalamus, unlike every other sense. How should that claim be evaluated?

options.text: The claim is accurate about smell
The claim is wrong because smell uses the thalamus
options.misconception: reverses the known routing of olfaction relative to other senses

options.text: The claim is wrong because touch also bypasses it
options.misconception: extends the exception to touch, which is relayed through it

options.text: The claim is wrong because smell uses the cerebellum
options.misconception: names a coordination structure as the olfactory relay point

questions.hint: Ask which sense is the documented exception.

questions.stem: A nerve leaves the brainstem to carry signals to structures of the head and neck. Which classification fits that nerve best?

options.text: A cranial nerve
A spinal nerve

options.text: A central tract
options.misconception: confuses a bundle inside the brain with a nerve leaving it

questions.explanation: Cranial nerves emerge directly from the brain or brainstem, while spinal nerves emerge from the cord. A ganglion is a relay cluster of cell bodies and a tract is a bundle inside the central nervous system, so neither describes a nerve leaving the brainstem.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain the balance of excitation and inhibition
questions.stem: Explain why the brain needs both excitatory and inhibitory transmitters, and what happens when the balance tips toward excess excitation.

answer.exemplar: Excitatory transmitters drive neurons toward firing so signals can be carried, and inhibitory transmitters hold them back so patterns of firing can be shaped and noise can be suppressed. Without inhibition, every activated cell would recruit everything it touches until activity swept outward without control. When the balance tips toward excess excitation, neurons fire in runaway bursts that appear as seizures, which is why substances that enhance inhibition are used to stop them. The balance is the substrate of both accurate signaling and protection from overload.

questions.explanation: Excitation supplies the signal and inhibition supplies the shaping and the brake. Tip the balance toward excitation and activity escalates into seizure, which is why inhibitory transmitters are clinically important.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to firing if nothing ever said stop.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a person who takes a sedative daily for months needs a larger dose for the same effect, and why stopping abruptly can be dangerous.

answer.exemplar: Regular exposure causes the nervous system to compensate: receptor numbers fall, receptor sensitivity drops, and the pathways that opposed the drug become more active. Because of that adaptation the same dose now produces a smaller effect, so more is needed to reach the original state. When the drug is removed, the compensatory changes remain, so the system overshoots in the opposite direction, producing withdrawal symptoms that can include tremor, agitation, and dangerous overactivity of the nervous system. That rebound is why such drugs are tapered rather than stopped abruptly.

questions.explanation: Tolerance comes from compensatory adaptation, and removing the drug exposes those adaptations as an unopposed opposite state. The overshoot is why abrupt cessation is hazardous and why doses are reduced gradually.
questions.hint: Consider what the body does to restore balance while the drug is present.

Non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension
options.misconception: mismatches fluent but empty speech to the slow, effortful pattern

options.text: Pure word-blindness with intact hearing
options.misconception: names a reading deficit rather than a comprehension one

options.text: Motor apraxia affecting the speech muscles
options.misconception: attributes the deficit to movement planning rather than language

questions.hint: Look at whether speech is fluent or effortful, and whether comprehension is spared.

questions.stem: A table records test results for a person whose hemisphere-connecting fibers have been cut: with an image flashed only in the left visual field, the person cannot name it verbally but can reach for it with the left hand. What do the results indicate?

options.text: Each hemisphere can act on information it receives alone
The right hemisphere produces all speech
options.misconception: assigns language output to the hemisphere that received the image

options.text: The left hemisphere controls the left hand
options.misconception: reverses the contralateral control of each hand

options.text: The person is blind in the left visual field
options.misconception: denies vision that the reaching response clearly demonstrates

questions.explanation: The right hemisphere saw the object and directed the left hand, while the speech-dominant left hemisphere never learned what it was, so naming failed. questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why autonomic output to an organ uses two neurons in a chain rather than one, and where the first neuron's cell body sits.

answer.exemplar: The first neuron leaves the central nervous system and ends in a ganglion outside it, where it synapses with the second neuron that runs the last distance to the target organ. Ganglia sit close to the organs, which lets many central fibers fan out to different targets and lets local modulation adjust the output before it arrives. The cell body of the first neuron sits inside the central nervous system, in the brainstem or spinal cord, and the second neuron's cell body sits in the ganglion. This arrangement allows coordination across organs from a central source.

questions.explanation: The two-neuron chain places a synapse in an accessible ganglion between the central source and the organ, allowing both divergence and local modulation. The first cell body is inside the central nervous system and the second sits in the ganglion.
questions.hint: Locate the synapse between the two neurons, then name where each cell body sits.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain dopamine in motor and reward pathways
questions.stem: Explain how the same messenger can contribute to smooth movement and to reward learning, and what damage to its midbrain source produces.

answer.exemplar: One group of dopamine cells in the midbrain sends fibers to the basal ganglia, where the messenger facilitates the initiation of movement, and another group projects to forebrain regions involved in reward and prediction of outcomes. Movement becomes labored and tremulous when the movement-facing projection degenerates, which is why patients with that condition struggle to start walking. Reward prediction relies on changes in dopamine release when an outcome differs from what was expected, so the same chemical supports both smooth action and learning about what leads to what. Its effect depends on which pathway is speaking.

questions.explanation: Dopamine acts in parallel loops, one supporting movement initiation and another tagging outcomes worth repeating. Damage to the movement-facing loop produces tremor and difficulty initiating motion, while the reward loop stays available for learning.
questions.hint: Name the two projection systems and what each contributes.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim about transmitter release
questions.stem: A researcher claims that a drug's effect proves it must be acting on the postsynaptic receptor, since that is where the response is measured. How should that claim be judged?

Sound, because only receptor channels control responses

options.misconception: denies that altering release changes the postsynaptic response

questions.stem: A diagram shows two pathways from skin to muscle. One path loops through the spinal cord only; the other ascends to motor cortex before descending. Which statement about the two is correct?

The short path is slower because it skips the brain

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a transmitter with several receptor subtypes can produce different drug effects when each subtype is targeted separately.

answer.exemplar: One transmitter is matched by several receptor proteins, and each protein activates a different set of channels and internal cascades, so each subtype produces a different downstream effect. A compound that fits and activates only one subtype therefore triggers only that subtype's effect and leaves the rest of the system untouched. A compound that fits several subtypes produces an effect that is the sum of the separate repertoires, which explains why similar messengers can yield quite different outcomes depending on which receptor is in play.

questions.explanation: Receptor subtype determines the downstream effect, so targeting subtypes selectively changes which effects appear. That is why messengers can support different functions in different circuits even when the chemical itself is identical.
questions.hint: Start from which ion or cascade each subtype controls.

options.text: The cerebrospinal pathway

questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is the thick fiber tract joining the hemispheres so that each shares information with the other. The reticular formation regulates arousal, the limbic structures handle emotion and memory, and cerebrospinal fluid is not a connecting bundle of nerve fibers.
questions.hint: The name literally calls a body of tissue.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why damage to the left frontal lobe is more likely to produce speech difficulty than equivalent damage on the right side.

answer.exemplar: Language is lateralized, meaning its core production and comprehension areas sit in the left hemisphere for most right-handed people and for many left-handed people as well. Speech production in particular sits in the left frontal lobe, so a lesion there directly damages the machinery of fluent output. Equivalent right-sided damage lands on structures that mainly support attention, spatial judgment, and emotional tone, so speech survives even when other abilities change. The asymmetry is why one hemisphere's stroke can take away language while the other's leaves it intact.

questions.explanation: Language functions are concentrated in the left hemisphere, so left frontal damage strikes the production area itself. The right hemisphere's roles do not include fluent speech, which is why equivalent right-sided damage spares language.
questions.hint: Ask which hemisphere usually holds speech production.

questions.stem: A table reports reflex latencies: 20 milliseconds for a myelinated withdrawal pathway, 80 milliseconds for an unmyelinated slow pain pathway, and 30 milliseconds for a motor command to the same muscle. What does the comparison show?

options.text: Myelinated fibers conduct signals faster
Faster latencies mean larger signals

options.text: All pathways in the table conduct equally fast
options.misconception: denies the fourfold spread in the recorded latencies

questions.hint: Compare the numbers rather than interpreting them as sizes.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain acetylcholine receptors at the junction
questions.stem: Explain what happens at the neuromuscular junction when released acetylcholine is cleared from the synaptic cleft, and why clearing it matters.

answer.exemplar: Acetylcholine released from the motor terminal binds receptors on the muscle fiber and opens channels that depolarize it, which triggers contraction. An enzyme in the cleft, acetylcholinesterase, promptly breaks the transmitter apart so that the muscle fiber repolarizes and the contraction ends. Without that breakdown, channels would stay open, the fiber would sit in a depolarized state, and it would stop responding to further signals. Clearing the transmitter is therefore as necessary for control as releasing it was for contraction.

questions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase clears the transmitter so the muscle fiber can relax and be ready for the next signal. Prolonged depotentiation makes the fiber unresponsive, which is why blocking the enzyme is both interesting clinically and hazardous.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the channels if the transmitter is never broken apart.

questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of blocking a channel
questions.stem: A compound blocks the potassium channels that normally open during repolarization. What happens to the shape of the next action potential?

options.text: It falls slowly and the membrane stays positive longer
It rises more quickly than before
options.misconception: assigns potassium channels the rising phase of the spike

options.text: The spike is unchanged because potassium is minor
options.misconception: understates the role of potassium efflux in resetting voltage

options.text: The spike fires repeatedly without a refractory period
options.misconception: claims no refractory period when depolarization prolongs it

questions.explanation: Potassium efflux drives repolarization, so blocking those channels leaves positive charge inside and the spike falls slowly. The rising phase is sodium-driven, potassium is central to the fall, and a prolonged positive phase lengthens rather than removes the refractory period.
questions.hint: Ask which ion leaves the cell to bring the voltage back down.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how a small local depolarization becomes a full action potential, describing the role of the trigger zone.

answer.exemplar: A local input opens some sodium channels, letting a little sodium in and moving the membrane closer to threshold. As depolarization reaches the trigger zone, where sodium channels are dense, enough channels open to make the influx self-reinforcing: sodium entry opens more channels, which admits more sodium. That regenerative wave continues until the inside swings positive and the sodium channels inactivate. The trigger zone governs whether this happens because its channel density makes it the region most likely to be pushed past threshold by any summed input.

questions.explanation: The trigger zone is where summed depolarization first crosses threshold, and its dense sodium channels make the entry of sodium self-reinforcing. Once that regenerative loop begins, the full spike follows automatically.
questions.hint: Describe the feedback loop and where it starts.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how one synapse can make it harder for a neuron to fire even though the synapse itself is active.

answer.exemplar: The synapse releases a transmitter that opens channels for a negatively charged ion, which enters the postsynaptic cell and moves its membrane further from threshold. In some cases the same transmitter holds potassium in or closes a depolarizing channel, which achieves the same shift. The neuron is now harder to trigger because more excitatory input is needed to reach threshold, so the active inhibitory synapse reduces firing without producing any signal of its own. The key point is that activity at a synapse means release and binding, not excitation.

questions.explanation: Inhibitory synapses drive the membrane away from threshold, so activity there reduces the chance of firing. Being released is not the same as being excitatory, which is why a synapse can be active and still make a response less likely.
questions.hint: Ask what the released transmitter does to the membrane voltage.

questions.hint: Ask which structure acts as the gatekeeper of wakefulness.

questions.stem: One class of transmitters is released broadly and slowly changes the responsiveness of whole circuits, while another opens specific channels at one synapse for a millisecond. What is the broad, slow-acting class called?

options.text: Neuromodulators
Ionotropic messengers
options.misconception: names fast channel-opening receptors rather than a broad class

options.text: Inhibitory neurotransmitters
options.misconception: confuses breadth and speed with the cell effect produced

options.text: Synaptic vesicles

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain what prevents an action potential from traveling backward along the axon it has just traversed.

answer.exemplar: Once a stretch of membrane fires, its sodium channels are inactivated and cannot fire again until they recover, so the stretch just traveled is temporarily unresponsive while the stretch ahead is still ready. The impulse therefore can only move forward into fresh membrane, because the region behind cannot be re-excited. If there were no refractory period, the local currents could re-excite the region behind the spike and the signal could reverberate or travel in both directions, scrambling the message.

questions.explanation: Sodium channel inactivation behind the spike makes re-excitation impossible in the region already passed, so the signal advances only into ready membrane. The refractory period therefore both enforces direction and sets a ceiling on firing rate.
questions.hint: Ask what the membrane behind the spike is doing while the region ahead is still excitable.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a reflex arc is protective
questions.stem: Explain why routing a withdrawal reflex through the spinal cord rather than through the brain improves the chance of avoiding injury.

answer.exemplar: The route from skin to spinal cord to muscle is short and involves few synapses, so it runs in fractions of a second. Routing through the brain would add the delay of ascending and descending pathways plus conscious interpretation before any movement could begin. Because tissue damage from heat or a sharp object accumulates with contact time, the shorter route shortens the exposure and reduces injury. The brain still receives the signal and becomes aware of the pain, but only after the movement has already started.

questions.explanation: Fewer synapses and a shorter path mean a faster reaction, and speed is protective when contact with a damaging stimulus is what causes harm. The brain is informed, but its involvement would slow the response.
questions.hint: Compare the number of synapses and the distance traveled in each route.

questions.hint: Ask which term describes needing the drug to feel normal.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how a person whose connecting fibers between the hemispheres have been cut can name an object seen by both eyes but can only point to it with the left hand when it is seen by the left visual field alone.

answer.exemplar: With both eyes open, each visual field reaches both hemispheres and speech-dominant left cortex receives the information, so naming is possible. With an image confined to the left visual field, it reaches only the right hemisphere, which cannot pass the information to the language areas on the left because the connecting fibers are cut. The right hemisphere can still direct the left hand, because it controls that side of the body, so the person can reach for the object with the left hand even though they cannot say what it is.

questions.explanation: Seeing to the right hemisphere and speaking from the left are disconnected when the joining fibers are cut, producing the dissociation between pointing and naming. Each hemisphere acts on what it receives, but only the left produces speech.
questions.hint: Track which hemisphere receives the image and which controls the hand.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how a transmitter is produced, stored, and released, and why the stored form is usually a precursor rather than the finished molecule.

answer.exemplar: The transmitter or its precursor is built from raw materials delivered to the terminal by the cell body or taken up locally, and enzymes in the terminal convert it into the finished form. It is then packed into vesicles by transporter proteins, which keep it concentrated and bundle it into single releasable units. When calcium enters at an impulse, vesicles fuse and empty their contents into the cleft. Storing a precursor or an enzyme-dependent route allows local control of how much active transmitter exists, which helps the synapse regulate its output without rebuilding protein.

questions.explanation: Synthesis, packaging, and calcium-triggered release form a chain, and storing a precursor or a controlled active form keeps the terminal able to adjust supply. The point is that release depends on a supply that has already been manufactured and bundled.
questions.hint: Name each step from raw material to release.

options.text: Improved coordination and balance
options.misconception: attributes motor gains to sedation of inhibition

options.text: Sharpened hearing alongside drowsiness
options.misconception: invents a sensory gain paired with a sedative effect

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a myelinated axon uses less energy per impulse than an unmyelinated axon of the same length.

answer.exemplar: Myelin prevents sodium and potassium from crossing the membrane along the wrapped internodes, so ions only move at the nodes of Ranvier. Each action potential therefore pumps fewer ions back across the membrane, and the sodium-potassium pump has less work to do. Energy is spent restoring ion gradients after they collapse, so the smaller the collapse, the smaller the cost of the next impulse. The same insulation that speeds conduction also reduces the metabolic price the cell pays for each signal.

questions.explanation: Restoring gradients after an impulse costs energy, and myelin limits the leak so fewer ions move during a spike. That is why insulated fibers are both fast and cheap to run.
questions.hint: Ask where ions move and how that changes what the pump must restore.

questions.stem: A record shows two inputs on the same neuron: the first moves the membrane from minus 70 to minus 60, and the second from minus 70 to minus 80. What will the first input do to firing probability relative to rest?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how a voluntary command reaches a muscle, naming the division and the transmitter at the endpoint.

answer.exemplar: A voluntary command travels from motor cortex down pathways in the somatic division of the peripheral nervous system to motor neurons that leave the spinal cord. Those motor neurons send axons out to the muscle fibers and release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, where the transmitter opens channels on the fiber and triggers contraction. The chain runs from planning regions through the somatic motor pathway to an acetylcholine-mediated endpoint, so each joint of the chain is either central or somatic, never autonomic.

questions.explanation: Voluntary movement uses the somatic motor division and ends in acetylcholine release at the muscle, which depolarizes the fiber and triggers contraction. Autonomic branches serve organs rather than skeletal muscle.
questions.hint: Name the division and then the transmitter at the endpoint.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how overactivity of the midbrain dopamine pathway could produce false perceptions, and why dampening dopamine can reduce them.

answer.exemplar: Dopamine in the reward-facing midbrain pathway signals significance and drives what becomes a salient perception. When that pathway is overactive, ordinary experiences may be tagged as significant and start to feel externally generated rather than self-produced, which shows up as false perceptions. Blocking dopamine receptors reduces that tagging, so fewer ordinary events become charged and the false perceptions fade. The tradeoff is that the same receptors in the movement pathway are also blocked, which produces movement side effects.

questions.explanation: Excess dopamine tags ordinary experience as significant, which can become false perception; receptor blockade reduces the tagging. The movement side effects come from blocking the same receptors in the movement-facing pathway.
questions.hint: Connect dopamine's signaling role to what it tags, then to what blockade removes.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why some compounds that act strongly on the peripheral nervous system have little effect on brain signaling.

answer.exemplar: Vessels of the brain are lined with cells joined tightly together, which block many molecules from slipping out of the blood into brain tissue. A compound that acts well on a cell in the body may be unable to cross that lining, so it never reaches its receptors in the central nervous system. Compounds that do cross tend to be small, lipid soluble, or carried by dedicated transporters. Whether a drug affects the brain therefore depends as much on getting in through this barrier as on matching its receptor.

questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier blocks many compounds from reaching brain tissue, so receptor affinity alone does not determine a central effect. Only molecules that cross the lining can act on central receptors.
questions.hint: Ask what separates blood from brain tissue.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a neuron cannot fire at an unlimited rate, and what determines its maximum frequency.

answer.exemplar: After each spike, sodium channels are inactivated and potassium continues to leave, so the membrane needs time to return toward its resting value before another spike can be triggered. The absolute refractory period sets a hard boundary, because no amount of stimulus can open inactivated sodium channels, while the relative period adds a further delay because the membrane is displaced. Larger and faster neurons recover sooner and fire at higher rates than small slow ones. The ceiling is therefore set by how quickly the channels and the voltage recover.

questions.explanation: Recovery time rather than stimulus strength sets the rate ceiling, and that recovery depends on channel dynamics and membrane properties. That is why maximum firing frequencies differ between neurons.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen after a spike before the next one is possible.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of calcium at the terminal
questions.stem: Explain why blocking calcium entry at a nerve terminal stops transmitter release within a few impulses, even though vesicles are still full.

answer.exemplar: Vesicles are docked and filled but remain inert until calcium enters the terminal and binds the proteins that fuse them with the membrane. Without calcium, the fusion machinery is not triggered, so the release-ready pool drains within a handful of impulses and then signaling stops. The vesicles themselves are unaffected, which is why restoring calcium restores release almost immediately. The lesson is that release is gated by an ion signal rather than by vesicle availability alone.

questions.explanation: Calcium is the trigger that converts docked vesicles into released transmitter, so removing it empties the release-ready pool even though storage remains intact. That is why the failure is fast and reversible.
questions.hint: Ask what converts a full vesicle into a released one.
